keep: The two terms are the right ones and named once each: domain (inputs taken) and range (outputs given), with HELM [^1] on the range.
The shadow picture follows OpenStax's own reading (inputs shown on the x-axis, outputs on the y-axis) and makes the range something you can see.
The two refused inputs are the ones the research names, dividing by zero and the square root of a negative [^2], on the one-over and the square root that lesson 3 already drew.
The 4 to 20 mA transmitter from lesson 2 is reused with its numbers (0.16 mA per percent, S(25) = 8, S(75) = 16), so nothing new has to be learned to read its shadows.
The dimmer is a new analogy (lesson 1 used the circuit chart, lesson 2 the chart recorder, lesson 3 the scope) from Dan's trade.
fix: False absolute: 'The domain always includes every number except the ones that cause dividing by zero...' fails on the transmitter itself, whose domain is 0 to 100%. Say that when nothing else limits it, the domain is every real input the rule can work on, and that the situation can limit it further.

Causal step skipped: why 1/x has no output at 0 (no number times 0 gives 1), why √x refuses negatives (a positive times a positive and a negative times a negative are both positive), and why x² never gives a negative. Each needs its one-line reason.
Causal step skipped: why the range is the harder half. Show the square on −2 to 3, whose ends give 4 and 9 while the curve dips to 0 in between, so reading the ends gives 4 to 9 instead of 0 to 9.

Misconception not caught: the y-axis trap (ERIC ED599786, notes 6.8), reaching for a turning point's height on the output axis when asked for the domain. Add a DO screen with a sketched hump whose top sits on the output axis.
Misconception not caught: thinking √x refuses 0. Say √0 = 0 and draw the edge as a filled dot, with a DO slip for it.
The one-over's range has a gap at 0 too (1 divided by any number is never 0). It is the clearest case of the harder range and is missing.

Asymptote is in the brief (SQA's HN unit asks for it) but not taught. Describe the curve getting ever closer to the axis first, then name it once, unfootnoted as textbooks' word since no source in RESEARCH defines it.

The 12 mA line is dropped in without the reason and without the square root's domain and range: tie it to the flow meter as a square-root rule with a domain set by the cell's span, both bands 0 to 1, and the 50% point landing at 71% [^3]. Cite the transmitter's straight-line rule [^7].
Text talks about the idea instead of teaching it: explain is a list of results. Rewrite as 3-4 paragraphs, each step following from the last, ending on a takeaway that keeps 'not from its ends'.

Recommended shape: practice lacks steps that work, a rule of thumb, a fully worked example with computed numbers (12 V through 3 to 12 Ω, 4 A down to 1 A, ends swapped) and the real mistakes (swapping the two, ends only, y-axis point, √0).

Analogy reproduces only half the result and its 'breaks' is one clause: say the knob's travel is the domain, the brightnesses the range, that some dimmers never reach off (a range need not start at 0), and that a domain can lose one point in the middle, as 0 on the one-over, which no knob does.

whatAmILookingAt does not tell the builder the twelve screens, each family's drawn inputs, the hollow hole, the filled edge, the arrows for bands that run on, or the puzzles and slips. ignores is too thin: name every example value, the hump as a sketch, real numbers only (Complex numbers later).

numbers is missing most values: the 0 to 100% scale, S(100) = 20, the square's −3 to 3 and −2 to 3, the one-over's −4 to 4 and its 100 from 0.01, the root's 0 to 9 and −4, the hump's −4 to 4, 6 and 2, the 12 V, 3 Ω and 12 Ω, and −0.25.
